source.title: Zenith: Scaling up Ranking Models for Billion-scale Livestreaming Recommendation
source.authors: Ruifeng Zhang; Ze-Xi Huang; Zi-Kai Wang; Ke Sun; Bo Zheng; Yu-Chen Jiang; Zhe Chen; Zhen Ouyang; Huimin Xie; P. Shen; Jun-Lin Zhang; Yu-Chao Zheng; Wen-Tao Guo; Qing-Lei Wang

page_placements.theme: Recommendation scaling depends on backbone, history and feature handling

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. The conference and DOI details contain template placeholders, but the paper is otherwise readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates model scaling in a recommendation-ranking setting, reporting LogLoss at multiple parameter and inference-compute scales. This is a new training/application regime relative to language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The study reports ranking-model LogLoss across sizes and compute budgets, not held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy or fitted power-law exponents. It does not report extrapolation from small runs or a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. The token-similarity measurements and online business metrics do not directly measure a claim version.
record.test_reason: This is an architecture paper. It proposes Zenith/Zenith++ ranking models and compares them with DCN-V2, DHEN and Wukong at three size tiers (about 100M, 500M and 1B parameters) on one production CTR dataset. The tiers span about one order of magnitude, and no power law is fitted, no exponent is reported and nothing is extrapolated. 'Superior scaling laws' is used informally to mean larger LogLoss gains per tier than the baselines. The results measure the study's own method against others, not whether the power-law form holds in recommendation models.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly correct. The authors conclude that Zenith and Zenith++ outperform the DCN-V2, DHEN and Wukong baselines at every tested scale, scaling better in both parameters and inference FLOPs. They credit tokenwise parameterisation that preserves token heterogeneity. They also report a month-long online A/B test of Zenith++ (383M/916M) against the DCN-V2 baseline: +1.05% CTR AUC, -1.10% LogLoss, and +9.93% / +8.11% in quality watch sessions and duration per user.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates recommendation-ranking architectures on production interaction data, comparing model sizes and inference FLOPs. It does not reproduce language-model pretraining, power-law fitting, or compute-optimal token/parameter allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Scaling outcomes differ across architecture families: the paper describes DCN-V2 as saturating beyond 100M parameters, Wukong as giving modest gains, and Zenith variants as scaling more effectively.

fits_no_version.finding: In CTR ranking models, LogLoss gains from scaling depend strongly on architecture. DCN-V2 is flat from 98.5M to 1050M parameters (.08237 to .08235). The Zenith variants keep improving (Zenith++ .08214 to .08188 between the small and large tiers).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether recommendation ranking-model loss improves with parameter count depends on architecture; some families saturate near 100M parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: Non-tokenwise SwiGLU/SMoE variants saturated after 50M parameters. Doubling parameters via token dimension, token count or layer count gave no gain, which the authors attribute to token homogenisation (Sec. 4.3). The text gives no numbers for this.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ranking-model scaling saturates when token representations homogenise across layers.

record.problems: The study reports one production ranking dataset and no uncertainty estimates. It does not fit power laws, report exponents, or test extrapolation; the scale results therefore do not establish the functional form stated in V5.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant LogLoss scale results were left out. Other reported metrics and ablations were omitted because they do not directly measure the claim versions; token-similarity results are in Figure 4, ablations in Table 3, and online metrics in Table 4.

untested.parts: Whether a power-law form holds for recommendation ranking models. Three size tiers per architecture are reported with no fit, no exponent and no data-size axis.
Not studied; no language-model pretraining loss is reported.
Not studied; no extrapolation from small runs.
Not studied for language models. The non-tokenwise depth/width changes described are ranking models and are reported without numbers.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's relation 'tests' (T3) with a V5 limits_scope label is downgraded to T4. The rows compare the proposed method with baselines across three size tiers, with no power-law fitting, so they cannot show V5's functional form. Kaplan et al. is cited only as motivation. One production dataset is used, no uncertainty is reported, and the sparse embedding table is excluded from parameter counts.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss of language models and its power-law relation to parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger-run loss from power laws fitted on small runs.
A fixed-compute search over parameter and token allocation, and stable power-law growth of the compute-optimal split.
Controlled comparison of language-model architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study evaluates recommendation-ranking models, but does not fit or verify the same power-law form, report exponents, or test image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Predictability of language-model downstream-task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, and bending away from fitted power laws.

relation.reason: The study uses scaling as an architectural design premise and reports method performance; its scaling comparisons do not establish any defined claim version.

tranche.reason: Scaling motivates the proposed ranking architectures; the experiments compare their performance across size and inference-compute tiers without testing a catalog claim version's power-law form, extrapolation, allocation, or fitted exponents.

source_check.notes: Parameter comparisons exclude the shared sparse embedding table; Zenith++ counts distinguish active from total parameters. The authors describe superior scaling, but provide no power-law fit or exponent.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports different scaling outcomes by architecture, including stated DCN-V2 saturation and larger gains for Zenith variants, but does not fit or verify a shared power-law form; see r1–r15.
